questions.question: Net gravitational force at the center of a square is found to be $F_{1}$ when four particles having mass $M, 2 M, 3 M$ and $4 M$ are placed at the four corners of the square as shown in figure and it is $F_{2}$ when the positions of $3 M$ and $4 M$ are interchanged. The ratio $\frac{F_{1}}{F_{2}}$ is $\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{5}}$. The value of $\alpha$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
Let $k = \frac{G}{r^2\sqrt{2}}$ where $r = a/\sqrt{2}$.
Net field at center has components along $x$ and $y$.
Config 1 (original):
$g_x = k(-M+2M+3M-4M) = 0$,
$g_y = k(-M-2M+3M+4M) = 4kM$.
$F_1 = 4kM$.
Config 2 (3M and 4M swapped):
$g_x = k(-M+2M+4M-3M) = 2kM$,
$g_y = k(-M-2M+4M+3M) = 4kM$.
$F_2 = kM\sqrt{4+16} = 2\sqrt{5}\,kM$.
$\frac{F_1}{F_2} = \frac{4}{2\sqrt{5}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \Rightarrow \alpha = 2$.

questions.question: A planet has double the mass of the earth. Its average density is equal to that of the earth. An object weighing $W$ on earth will weigh on that planet:
questions.solution:
The formula for acceleration due to gravity is

$g = \dfrac{GM}{R2}$

Let the density of earth and planet be $ρ$, and the radius of the planet be $R '$. Let $R$ be the radius of the earth and $g$ be the acceleration due to gravity of earth and $g '$ be the acceleration due to gravity of planet.

So, the masses are

$M = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{R}^{3}ρ . . . ( i )$

$M ' = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi\left(R '\right)3ρ . . . ( ii )$

So, $\dfrac{g '}{g} = \dfrac{\dfrac{GM '}{R{'}^{2}}}{\dfrac{GM}{{R}^{2}}} = \dfrac{M '}{M}\left(\dfrac{R}{R '}\right)2 . . . ( iii )$

From equation (i) and (ii) we get $R ' = 2\dfrac{1}{3}R$

Substituting the value in equation (iii),

$\dfrac{g '}{g} = \left({2}^{1}\right)2\dfrac{- 2}{3} = 2\dfrac{1}{3}g$

Weight is given by $W ' = mg ' = 2\dfrac{1}{3}W$

Assume that the earth is a solid sphere of uniform density and a tunnel is dug along its diameter throughout the earth. It is found that when a particle is released in this tunnel, it executes a simple harmonic motion. The mass of the particle is $100g$. The time period of the motion of the particle will be (approximately)

(take $g = 10{ms}^{- 2}$, radius of earth $= 6400km$)
questions.solution:
The gravitational force acting on a particle of mass $m$ at a distance$r ( < R )$ from the centre of Earth is

$F = - G\dfrac{{M}^{'}m}{r2}$ ....(1)

where ${M}^{'}$ is the mass of portion of Earth enclosed by a sphere of radius $r$ concentric with Earth. Here $-$ sign indicates radially inward direction of force.

Taking the density of Earth to be uniform

$\dfrac{M '}{4{πr}^{3}} = \dfrac{M}{4{πR}^{3}}$

$⇒ {M}^{'} = \dfrac{M{r}^{3}}{R3}$ ....(2)

Substituting ${M}^{'}$ from equation 2 into equation 1:

$F = - \left(\dfrac{GMm}{R3}\right)r$

Which is similar to the equation of motion $F = - kx$ with $k = G\dfrac{Mm}{R3} = \dfrac{mg}{R} ( ∵ g = G\dfrac{M}{R2} )$

For such motion, the time period is given by:

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$

Substituting k from above,

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}}$

Putting the values, we get

$T = 2 \times 3 . 14\sqrt{\dfrac{6400 \times {10}^{3}}{10}} = 2 \times 3 . 14 \times 800 \approx 1hour24minutes$

When one moves from a point $16$ km below the earth's surface to a point $16$ km above the earth's surface. The change in $g$ is approximately $\alpha$ %. The value of $\alpha$ is _____.
(Take radius of the earth $= 6400$ km.)
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a depth $d$ below the earth's surface is given by:

$g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)$

The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the earth's surface (for $h \ll R$) is given by:

$g_h = g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)$

Given $d = 16$ km and $h = 16$ km, we can find the values of $g_d$ and $g_h$:

$g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{16}{6400}\right) = g\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{400}\right)$

$g_h = g\left(1 - \dfrac{2 \times 16}{6400}\right) = g\left(1 - \dfrac{2}{400}\right)$

The magnitude of the change in acceleration due to gravity when moving from the depth $d$ to the height $h$ is:

$\Delta g = g_d - g_h = g\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{400}\right) - g\left(1 - \dfrac{2}{400}\right)$

$\Delta g = g\left(\dfrac{2}{400} - \dfrac{1}{400}\right) = \dfrac{g}{400}$

The percentage change in $g$ is approximately:

$\dfrac{\Delta g}{g} \times 100 = \dfrac{\dfrac{g}{400}}{g} \times 100 = \dfrac{100}{400} = 0.25\%$

Thus, the value of $\alpha$ is $0.25$.

Answer: $0.25$

Work done equals negative change in gravitational potential energy.
For three masses in an equilateral triangle, gravitational PE is $U = -G\left(\frac{m_1m_2}{r_{12}} + \frac{m_2m_3}{r_{23}} + \frac{m_1m_3}{r_{13}}\right)$.
Initial configuration (side 20 m):
$U_i = -\frac{G}{20}(200 \times 300 + 300 \times 400 + 200 \times 400)$
$= -\frac{260000G}{20} = -13000G$
Final configuration (side 25 m):
$U_f = -\frac{G}{25}(260000) = -10400G$
Work done:
$W = -(U_f - U_i) = -10400G + 13000G$
$= 2600G = 2600 \times 6.7 \times 10^{-11}$
$= 1.742 \times 10^{-7}$ J $\approx 1.74 \times 10^{-7}$ J

questions.question: If a body of mass $1$ kg falls on the earth from infinity, it attains velocity $(v)$ and kinetic energy $(k)$ on reaching the surface of earth. The values of $v$ and $k$ respectively are _______. (Take radius of earth to be $6400$ km and $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$)
questions.solution:
By conservation of mechanical energy, the total energy of the body at infinity is zero.

When the body reaches the surface of the earth, its potential energy is $-\dfrac{GMm}{R}$ and kinetic energy is $k = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

$0 = k - \dfrac{GMm}{R}$

$k = \dfrac{GMm}{R} = mgR$

Substituting $m = 1$ kg, $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$, and $R = 6400 \times 10^3$ m:

$k = 1 \times 9.8 \times 6400 \times 10^3 = 6.272 \times 10^7$ J

The velocity $v$ is given by $\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = k$.

$v = \sqrt{2gR} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 6400 \times 10^3}$

$v = \sqrt{125.44 \times 10^6} = 11.2 \times 10^3$ m/s $= 11.2$ km/s

Answer: $11.2$ km/s; $6.27 \times 10^7$ J

For a satellite revolving around the Earth in a circular orbit, it can be written that

Similarly, for distance $r '$ from the centre of the Earth, the angular momentum is given by

Divide equation (3) by equation (2) to obtain the required angular momentum.

questions.question: Two planets $A$ and $B$ having masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ move around the sun in circular orbits of $r_1$ and $r_2$ radii respectively. If angular momentum of $A$ is $L$ and that of $B$ is $3 \mathrm{~L}$, the ratio of time period $\left(\frac{T_A}{T_B}\right)$ is:
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{\pi \mathrm{r}_1^2}{\mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{A}}}=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2 \mathrm{~m}_1} \ldots \ldots .(1) \\ & \frac{\pi \mathrm{r}_2^2}{\mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{3 \mathrm{~L}}{2 \mathrm{~m}_2} \ldots \ldots .(2) \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}}=3 \cdot \frac{\mathrm{m}_1}{\mathrm{~m}_2} \cdot\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right)^2 \\ & \left(\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)^2=\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right)^3 \Rightarrow\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right)^2=\left(\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)^{\frac{4}{3}} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{27} \cdot\left(\frac{\mathrm{m}_2}{\mathrm{~m}_1}\right)^3=\left(\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)\end{aligned}$
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{\pi \mathrm{r}_1^2}{\mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{A}}}=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2 \mathrm{~m}_1} \ldots \ldots .(1) \\ & \frac{\pi \mathrm{r}_2^2}{\mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{3 \mathrm{~L}}{2 \mathrm{~m}_2} \ldots \ldots .(2) \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}}=3 \cdot \frac{\mathrm{m}_1}{\mathrm{~m}_2} \cdot\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right)^2 \\ & \left(\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)^2=\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right)^3 \Rightarrow\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right)^2=\left(\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)^{\frac{4}{3}} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{27} \cdot\left(\frac{\mathrm{m}_2}{\mathrm{~m}_1}\right)^3=\left(\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)\end{aligned}$
